title: Nucleus — binding energy, nuclear fission and fusion
topicTitle: Nucleus — binding energy, nuclear fission and fusion
notes: The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its separated protons and neutrons. The difference is the mass defect. It is not a mistake in the weighing. It is the mass equivalent of the binding energy.
Binding energy = Δm c^2. In nuclear units, 1 u corresponds to 931 MeV. The binding energy is the energy you would have to supply to pull the nucleus apart into free nucleons.

The useful comparison between nuclei is the binding energy per nucleon, the total divided by the mass number A. It is low for the very light nuclei, highest near iron, and a little lower again for the heavy nuclei.
Fission splits a very heavy nucleus into two medium ones. Those pieces sit higher on the curve, so energy is released. A chain reaction needs neutrons from one fission to cause the next.

Fusion joins very light nuclei into a heavier one that is higher on the curve. That also releases energy. It is the energy source of the Sun. The nuclei must be brought close enough for the strong force to act, which means a very high temperature.
Both processes release energy for the same reason: the products have a larger binding energy per nucleon, so the products are lighter, and the missing mass has left as energy.

summary: A nucleus is lighter than its free nucleons by the mass defect, and that mass is the binding energy, with 1 u equal to 931 MeV. Stability follows the binding energy per nucleon, which peaks near iron. Fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei both move toward that peak and release energy.
